items.why_watch: Anthropologist Agustín Fuentes goes through viral AI-generated Stone Age content and pinpoints exactly where it goes wrong — not just fact-checking, but explaining *why* these myths spread so easily. It's a useful exercise in recognizing how plausible-sounding misinformation works, with a real expert doing the correcting rather than a generalist.

items.why_watch: Daniel Coyle, author of *The Talent Code*, pushes back on the mythology of individual genius by examining the hidden webs of mentorship, culture, and environment behind high achievement. At 85 minutes it's a long sit, but the full interview format lets him develop ideas that get flattened in shorter clips — worth it if you're drawn to questions about how skill and success actually develop.

items.title: On the Nature of Time According to Modern Physics - Jim Al-Khalili
items.description:
0:00 // Introduction — five chapters on the nature of time
2:08 // The philosophical problems — Parmenides vs Heraclitus
5:29 // Physical time — time as number, dimension and arrow
9:35 // What does it mean for time to flow?
12:46 // Laplace's demon and why the future is unpredictable
17:19 // Is time fundamental, emergent or just a measuring tool?
21:37 // The block universe — all moments coexist in spacetime
23:30 // Time dilation — GPS satellites, black holes and Interstellar
28:15 // Quantum
items.why_watch: Physicist Jim Al-Khalili walks through one of philosophy's hardest questions — what time actually *is* — with a clear chapter structure that moves from ancient philosophy to block universe theory without losing the thread. If you've ever bounced off dense treatments of this topic, his Gresham College style tends to be unusually accessible without sacrificing depth.

items.why_watch: Henry Woollett shot down six enemy aircraft in a single day in WWI — a feat obscure enough that most aviation history enthusiasts won't know his name. The History Guy does what he does best: rescues a specific, well-documented story from undeserved anonymity in a tight 14 minutes.

garden_note.note: September is doing its quiet work in Zürich tonight — the linden trees are releasing the last of their warmth, and the kitchen garden smells of damp earth and ripening squash as the air turns genuinely cool after dark. There's a particular pleasure in this early-autumn hush, when the days are still generous but dusk arrives just early enough to remind you that the season is gently turning the page.
